else.text: A rollercoaster. Down my pit. Ninety metres of the real dark, and they want to improve it with a scream track.

Their draft is pinned on the board by the door. Read it. Then go and see the Fed's old lodge workings off the east face. There's a tram of timber you'll have to shift. Don't ask who stacked it. It was 1936 and he's long retired.
Mind, the roads round there haven't been walked since before the war. Take the lamp and go gently.
A way through to the old lodge workings is open at the east end of the coal face.

then.text: Mind how you go. And never whistle underground.

else.text: Sing for the Eisteddfod? Me? Bass, forty years, down the pit and up the chapel. Right. One question first: which hymn, a favourite of choirs and rugby crowds, asks for a pure heart?
Which song asks for a 'pure heart'?

then.text: Calon Lan! 'Nid wy'n gofyn bywyd moethus': I do not ask for a life of luxury. Man after my own heart. Right, I'll sing.
You found a bass for the eisteddfod choir.

else.text: Not that one, bach. Think of the rugby crowd. Think of the second verse that nobody knows. Come back.
Ah, the one who went down on her own two feet. I mean theirs. Anyway, any time you want to see the pit again, I'm here.
Big Pit, the National Coal Museum. We do tours with ex-miners. We're the only place in Wales where the exhibits tell you off.

then.text: You've been down, you've heard them, you've even got one in the bag. Not many can do that. Most visitors just hear the guide.
Here, a Davy lamp. Not a working one. A charm. Sir Humphry Davy made the first in 1815 so a flame couldn't ignite the gas. You've got the sense of a collier.
And a wedge of Pwll Mawr, from the cheese, down the pit. It tastes better after you've been down.
Lamp on? Helmet on? Mind your head. The roof is lower than you think.
The cage doors clatter shut. The daylight shrinks to a postage stamp, then goes out. Ninety metres is a long way down, and it feels longer.

else.text: No rush. The coal's not going anywhere. It's had a few hundred million years.
First, the lamp room rules. It's the rules or nothing. What do you hand in before you go down the shaft?
What do you hand in at the lamp room?
options: Anything that could make a spark: matches, lighters, phones

then.text: Spot on. Methane collects in the roof and one spark in the wrong place is the end of the shift and then some.
Here's your lamp, and a hard hat, and a self-rescuer in case the air turns. You won't need it. Probably.

else.text: No, no, no. Think about what's underground with you. Gas. What does gas hate? A spark. Try again.
Bore da! Gwilym. I worked in this pit until it closed in 1980. Now I show people down it. Same pit, different hat.
Big Pit was sunk in 1860. Down the shaft, 90 metres, and a mile or more of tunnels. We go down in the cage with a lamp and a helmet. I won't lie to you: it's dark.
They say there are knockers down there: the coblynau, little men in the rock who tap out the way to the best seams. I've never seen one. I've heard something, mind. Fancy a look?
